title: Bhikhan's medicine
hook: Bhikhan calls the Name the medicine for every illness (Sorath, Bhikhan, ang 659)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaidev, the old poet: one Lord beyond compare, and purity in deed, word and thought. Your line was the old poet. Did those three point the same way, even once? Day seven hundred ninety.

The bathroom cabinet. Something for a headache, something for a cough, a half-used tube for a burn, a bottle with a date long gone. Every shelf has a cure for one particular thing. Bhagat Bhikhan, in Raag Sorath on Ang 659, writes from the other side of all those shelves: an old body, eyes running, voice failing. And he names a single medicine, and says it's for every illness. Not one shelf among many. One remedy, for all of it.
screen: `A CABINET OF CURES.` → `ONE FOR EACH THING.` → `ONE MEDICINE FOR EVERY ILLNESS.`

segments.voice: Bhikhan starts with the body, and he doesn't flatter it. In paraphrase: water streams from the eyes, the body has grown thin, the hair has turned white as milk. The throat is choked, and the words won't come out. And then the question to himself: what can you do now? It's an honest picture of old age, the kind of picture that is easy to look away from. Then he turns, and the doctor appears. In paraphrase: O Lord, my King, be the physician, and save your devotees. He doesn't ask God to stop him aging. He asks for a healer of a different kind. Then the hymn goes under the skin. In paraphrase: the head aches, the body burns, the heart is in pain, and this is a pain no medicine reaches. And then he names one. The Name of the Lord is pure nectar water, the finest medicine in all the world. In the hymn that follows, he calls that Name a jewel beyond price. Turn the picture a few ways. A medicine is something you take regularly, not once. It works from the inside. And it doesn't ask whether you deserve it. That's how Bhikhan speaks of the Name: remembered again and again, quietly, working where no ointment reaches. And it's worth being clear about what he isn't saying. The hymn doesn't tell anyone to throw out the cabinet, or to skip the doctor. Read this way, Bhikhan is talking about the ache underneath the aches: fear, restlessness, the sense of being far from God. For that, he names one medicine: the Name of the Lord.
screen: `EYES RUNNING, HAIR WHITE AS MILK.` · `LORD, BE THE PHYSICIAN.` · `THE NAME: JEWEL, NECTAR, MEDICINE.` · `NOT INSTEAD OF A DOCTOR: UNDER THE ACHES.` · then, large: `THE NAME AS MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: For the practice, take a quiet minute as medicine. In the sit, find the ache that isn't in a muscle. A worry, a restless loop, a heaviness. Don't fix it. Just let the breath come and go across it, slowly, the way you'd let a medicine work. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, like a dose taken again and again. If you don't, let the quiet itself be the dose. The bell holds the time.
Bhikhan's medicine. In Raag Sorath, an old devotee asks the Lord to be his physician, and calls the Name the medicine for every illness.
Your line: the name as medicine. Today, when a worry flares, take one quiet minute before you do anything else, and see what it does. Day seven hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Bhikhan's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Sorath, and Sikh teaching speaks of naam, remembering God's Name, as healing for the mind, alongside ordinary care for the body.

notes: Paraphrase of the first hymn (nainah neer bahai tan kheenaa bhae kes dudh vaanee; roodhaa kanth sabad nahee uchrai; raam raai hohi baid banvaaree apne santah leh ubaaree): confirm.

Paraphrase of the second hymn calling the Name a priceless jewel, pure nectar water and the medicine of the world for every illness: confirm the images, especially 'medicine' (aukhadh) and 'every illness' as the index hook states.
Line on doctors ('Sikhs go to doctors like anyone else') is added to keep the practice from implying medical advice; confirm wording.
Original-language game set to null: the Gurmukhi spelling of 'medicine' in this hymn (ਅਉਖਧੁ vs ਅਉਖਦੁ) was not certain.

Editor pass: replaced the sweeping 'Sikhs go to doctors like anyone else' and the unsourced 'it's free' ending with a plain statement that the hymn says nothing against doctors and names the Name as the medicine; varied the hook ending, a 'Here's' turn and the practice opener.

Audit (2026-10-01): the teach put 'nectar water' and 'medicine' in the second hymn; both are in the first (maathe peer sareer jalan hai ... vaa kaa aukhadh naahee; har kaa naam amrit jal nirmal ih aukhadh jag saaraa), and the priceless jewel is in the second. Fixed, and added the head, body and heart pain line. The text says the medicine of (or best in) the world; 'every illness' comes from the index and stays in the word, match and hook only.
